body.heading: The messenger of Marathon
paragraphs: In 490 BCE, Greek forces won a famous victory over a Persian army on the plain of Marathon, near Athens. Legend tells of a messenger — often named Pheidippides — who ran from the battlefield to Athens with the news of victory, a journey of roughly twenty-five miles.

When the modern Olympic Games began in Athens in 1896, organisers created a race in the legend's honour, running from Marathon to Athens. The marathon has been an Olympic event ever since, and the town's name now belongs to runners everywhere.

body.heading: Why 26.2 miles?
paragraphs: Early marathons varied in length, each city choosing its own route. At the London Olympics of 1908, the course was set at 26 miles plus 385 yards so the race could start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box at the stadium — 26.2 miles in total.

That oddly precise distance became the world standard in 1921 and remains the official marathon length today: 42.195 kilometres. Every “26.2” sticker on a car window is quoting a decision made for a king's view in 1908.

body.heading: Try it: a marathon of steps
paragraphs: You do not need to run one to borrow the idea. Set a family “marathon” of reading (26.2 pages), of laps around the park, or of minutes spent practising an instrument, spread across a week, and mark the miles off on a chart.
Or walk the story: find out how far 26.2 miles is from your front door, and name the place you would reach. The legend lands differently when the finish line is somewhere you know.

takeaway: Marathon is a place name that became a distance: every runner since 1896 has been retracing a messenger's route.
